I have been farming these 9 mu in Quzhou for half a century. My bones are getting old, but the land and I understand each other. Me and my wife still manage everything ourselves — we do not hire labor if we can help it, though some days I pay the neighbor’s son to run the rotary tiller or the sprayer when my back aches. Around here, the wheat-maize double crop is the only sensible system; everyone does it, and our well gives us water when we need it.

For the winter wheat, I will rotary till before sowing in October. I will buy improved wheat seed from the township supply shop — the same kind I have used for years because it resists lodging and gives steady grain. I will spread compound fertilizer as basal and topdress with urea, totaling about 10 kg of nitrogen, 4 kg of phosphorus, and 3 kg of potassium per mu. Wheat is thirsty, so I will irrigate three times from the well: once after sowing or before winter if the soil is dry, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I will spray four times in total — herbicide once, insecticide twice, and fungicide once when the weather turns humid.

For the summer maize, there is no time to waste after wheat harvest in early June. I will plant hybrid maize seed right away using no-tillage — that is how we do it here. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat; I will give it about 8 kg nitrogen, 3 kg phosphorus, and 2 kg potassium per mu. Two irrigations are enough — one when it is knee-high and one at the big-flare stage. Three sprays total: one herbicide and two insecticides. If the year is kind, I expect roughly 500 kg per mu from the wheat and a bit more from the maize.
